title: Herodias Wanted the Preacher Silenced Because He Wouldn’t Bless Her Relationship
paragraphs: Herodias Wanted the Preacher Silenced Because He Wouldn’t Bless Her Relationship
She didn’t hate John because he was cruel. She hated what his words forced everyone to confront: some relationships can feel worth defending and still stand condemned by the Word of God.
There are sermons people applaud.
And then there are sermons people want buried.
John the Baptist preached one of the shortest sermons imaginable to a powerful man.
No stage lights.
No carefully engineered introduction.
No attempt to protect his influence.
No rebranding of sin so nobody important would become uncomfortable.
Just a prophet, a king, a forbidden relationship—and one sentence that eventually helped put John’s head on a platter.
Mark records his confrontation with Herod Antipas:
“For John had said unto Herod, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife.” — Mark 6:18, KJV
Matthew preserves essentially the same confrontation:
“For John said unto him, It is not lawful for thee to have her.” — Matthew 14:4, KJV
The Greek is brutally direct:
Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.
Ouk exestin soi echein tēn gynaika tou adelphou sou.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
That matters.
John was not merely saying, “I personally disagree with your relationship.”
He was not offering a competing lifestyle preference.
He was declaring that Herod did not possess moral permission to continue as though God approved what God’s law condemned.
And Herodias hated him for it.
Mark 6:19 says:
“Therefore Herodias had a quarrel against him, and would have killed him; but she could not.”
The Greek is even more vivid:
Ἡ δὲ Ἡρῳδιὰς ἐνεῖχεν αὐτῷ
The verb ἐνέχω — enechō carries the sense of holding something against someone, bearing hostility, nursing a grievance.
John had become a living reminder of something Herodias desperately wanted treated as acceptable.
So understand the headline correctly.
Scripture does not record Herodias walking up to John and literally saying, “Bless my relationship.”
It tells us something more serious.
John publicly declared that the relationship was unlawful before God, and Herodias wanted the man making that declaration destroyed.
She could imprison the preacher.
But she could not make his message become false.
And that is where this ancient scandal becomes frighteningly modern.
Because sometimes we do not actually want God to tell us whether something is holy.
We have already decided we want it.
We simply want God to approve the decision afterward.
We want heaven’s signature beneath a contract we wrote without Him.
We want Scripture to comfort us without correcting us.
We want Jesus as Savior while quietly negotiating whether He must also be Lord.
And when the Word touches the one thing we refuse to surrender…
something inside us starts looking for ways to silence the preacher.
Maybe you have never imprisoned a prophet.
Maybe you have never demanded anyone’s execution.
But perhaps you stopped listening to the Christian friend who challenged you.
Perhaps you unfollowed the pastor who preached the verse you did not want to hear.
Perhaps you found another teacher who told you exactly what you hoped God would say.
Perhaps you learned to call conviction “judgment” whenever conviction came too close to the thing you loved.
Or maybe your battlefield is not a relationship at all.
Maybe it is money.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Adultery.
Gossip.
An unforgiving heart.
Secret messages your spouse would be devastated to discover.
A business practice you know is dishonest.
An addiction hidden behind a respectable Christian face.
A relationship with God maintained publicly while privately you are becoming someone you barely recognize.
This is where Herodias stops being merely a notorious woman in an ancient palace.
Her story becomes a mirror.
Because the terrifying question is not merely, “How could Herodias hate John so much?”
The terrifying question is:
What truth about my own life am I tempted to silence because obedience would cost me something I do not want to surrender?
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because there may be something you have been asking God to bless that He has actually been asking you to surrender.
John understood something much of modern Christianity is tempted to forget:
Love does not require lying to people about sin.
The same Bible that declares that “all have sinned” also declares that God loved the world enough to give His Son.
Biblical truth and biblical love are not enemies.
They meet perfectly at the cross.
The cross does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross says your sin mattered so much that Christ died—and that God loved sinners so deeply that Christ willingly came to save them.
This is why genuine Christian preaching cannot merely tell people, “Follow your heart.”
Scripture warns:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9, KJV
And Jesus does not merely decorate the desires we already possess.
He calls us to Himself.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” — Matthew 16:24, KJV
That word “deny” comes from the Greek ἀπαρνέομαι — aparneomai.
This is not Jesus asking for a minor adjustment.
Following Christ involves surrendering our claim to ultimate self-rule.
That is offensive to the flesh.
Because we want a Jesus who saves us without contradicting us.
A Jesus who forgives but never commands.
A Jesus who comforts but never confronts.
A Jesus who carries the cross so we never have to carry ours.
But that Jesus is not the Jesus of Scripture.
The biblical Jesus could look at a woman caught in devastating sexual sin without joining the crowd determined to destroy her—and still tell her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Look at those words.
Grace did not throw the stone.
Truth did not call the sin righteousness.
Jesus did neither of the cruel things human beings so often do.
He did not crush the sinner.
And He did not redefine the sin.
He offered mercy and called for transformation.
That is Gospel grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved.
Power to come home.
And maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear tonight.
Your scandal does not have to become your identity.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sexual history is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
Your affair is not beyond His forgiveness.
Your divorce is not beyond His compassion.
Your addiction is not beyond His power.
Your secret is not too filthy for His mercy.
Your hypocrisy is not too complicated for repentance.
Your years of running have not exhausted the invitation of Christ.
But grace is not God pretending darkness is light.
Grace is God entering our darkness to rescue us from it.
That is why Jesus began His public proclamation with a word modern ears sometimes resist:
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite.
“Repent.”
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness by becoming good enough.
You cannot.
Neither can I.
Repentance is turning toward the God whose grace meets sinners precisely because they cannot save themselves.
The Gospel is not:
Clean yourself up, and perhaps Jesus will accept you.
The Gospel is:
You could never cleanse yourself from sin, so Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
John the Baptist could expose Herod’s sin.
But John could not die as Herod’s Savior.
Jesus could.
John could point at darkness.
Jesus came as Light.
John could announce repentance.
Jesus could purchase redemption.
And here lies one of the saddest possibilities inside Herod’s story.
Mark tells us that Herod actually feared John, recognized him as righteous and holy, protected him for a time, and even listened to him.
Think about that.
Herod listened.
He was disturbed.
He was fascinated.
He knew something about John was different.
And still the moment came when protecting his pride mattered more than responding rightly to truth.
At his birthday banquet, Herod made a reckless oath after Herodias’s daughter danced before the guests.
She consulted her mother.
The request returned:
“The head of John the Baptist.”
And eventually the voice Herod had been listening to was carried into the room on a platter.
What a terrifying picture.
A man can listen to truth repeatedly and still never surrender to it.
You can enjoy sermons and remain unchanged.
You can save Christian videos and remain unrepentant.
You can know worship songs by heart while protecting the very sin Christ keeps touching.
You can cry during an altar call and still walk home clutching the chains Jesus told you to release.
You can admire the preacher…
and still silence the message.
That is why this article cannot end with Herodias.
It has to come to you.
And me.
What have we been protecting from God?
What relationship?
What habit?
What resentment?
What secret?
What ambition?
What version of ourselves?
What would happen if instead of asking, “How can I make Scripture agree with me?” we finally whispered:
“Lord Jesus, make me agree with You.”
That prayer can hurt.
Because surrender often feels like death before it feels like freedom.
But Christ never calls us away from sin because He wants less life for us.
Sin promises life and eventually produces slavery.
Jesus calls slaves into freedom.
Maybe you are reading this with tears forming because you already know what God has been confronting.
You do not need another argument.
You need courage to surrender.
Then surrender.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret meeting.
Not after one more night.
Not after you clean yourself up enough to feel worthy.
Come to Christ now.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess what you have done.
Stop defending what He has exposed.
Ask for mercy.
Trust Christ.
Seek godly help where necessary.
Make restitution where biblical wisdom requires it.
Walk away from what must be abandoned.
And when you fall, do not make peace with the mud.
Run back to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of flawless people proving how righteous they are.
It is the story of guilty people discovering that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Peter had scandal.
The Samaritan woman had scandal.
The Corinthian church had scandal.
Paul carried a past stained with persecution and blood.
Yet the Gospel kept doing what the Gospel does.
Grace entered stories sin seemed to have ruined.
And Jesus rewrote everything.
That does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
It means sin no longer gets the final word over the person who belongs to Christ.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
No condemnation does not mean no conviction.
Conviction draws us toward repentance.
Condemnation tells us to hide from God.
The Gospel tells us to come into the light because Christ has already done what sinners could never do for themselves.
Do not merely admire John’s courage.
Ask whether you have been behaving like Herodias toward the truth.
Do not merely condemn Herod’s compromise.
Ask where compromise has been growing inside you.
Do not merely praise Jesus for saving sinners.
Ask whether you have actually surrendered to Him.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest enough to say it.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence that repentance is not the end of a person’s story.
It can be the beginning of coming home.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Let sharing become ministry rather than performance.
We glorify God fundamentally through Christ-centered faith and obedience.
You are helping truth travel.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior by following the page for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend quietly losing faith.
Invite the Christian who has become spiritually numb.
Invite the person ashamed to return to church.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who thinks their scandal has disqualified them forever.
Use them.
Share them.
Put biblical resources into the hands of people who need them.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is trying desperately to silence the voice telling them to repent.
But perhaps what feels like an interruption is actually mercy.
Perhaps conviction is not God abandoning you.
Perhaps it is evidence that you are still being called home.
Herodias wanted the preacher silenced because his message threatened what she wanted to keep.
Herod listened to the preacher but ultimately surrendered to something else.
And John lost his head without changing his message.
But even John was never the hero of the Gospel.
Jesus is.
The Lamb of God John had pointed toward eventually walked toward His own execution.
John's head was placed on a platter because powerful sinners wanted his voice silenced.
Jesus was nailed to a cross according to God's redemptive purpose, bearing sin for sinners.
And death could not silence Him.
The tomb could not hold Him.
The scandal of your past cannot overpower His grace.
So stop asking Jesus merely to bless the story you have already written.
Give Him the pen.
Give Him the relationship.
Give Him the addiction.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him the hidden room.
Give Him the reputation you have exhausted yourself protecting.
Give Him the future.
Give Him you.
Because there is something infinitely better than getting God to approve everything we want.
There is being forgiven, redeemed, transformed, and finally learning to want Him.
The truth you are most tempted to silence may be the very mercy Jesus is using to call you home.
